messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Callbacks in Stan?
parts:
I'll start with the use-case. In RStan, there's a function called 'run_markov_chain()' that mirrors Stan's function. I'd post the code, but it's not really useful as is. The substantive difference between the two functions is that RStan has one additional line:

    R_CheckUserInterrupt();

RStan calls that function to check whether or not the user has interrupted the process within a for loop. (For the time being, I'm going to ignore the danger in leaving dangling resources. This is how RStan currently works now and I'm just trying to refactor the code so we share more common code.)

My question is, should I just add a function pointer to the method to deal with this interrupt handler? Is there a different pattern we should adopt to make it cleaner?

Is this going to introduce too much overhead? What's the cleanest way to deal with an empty function? CmdStan doesn't need this call, so what should we do about it? Do I create two functions in Stan to maintain efficiency at the cost of duplicating code (one with and without this argument)?


Daniel

minimal.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Callbacks in Stan?
parts:
I see. I still think that logic can be pushed into Stan.

Let's get down to the implementation level, then. Here's RStan's function:
    template <class Model, class RNG_t>
    void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler_ptr,
                          const stan_args& args,
                          bool is_warmup,
                          mcmc_output<Model>& outputter,
                          stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
                          Model& model,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& chains,
                          int& iter_save_i,
                          const std::vector<size_t>& qoi_idx,
                          std::vector<double>& sum_pars,
                          double& sum_lp,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& sampler_params,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& iter_params,
                          std::string& adaptation_info,
                          RNG_t& base_rng) {
      int start = 0;
      int end = args.get_ctrl_sampling_warmup();
      if (!is_warmup) {
        start = end;
        end = args.get_iter();
      }
      for (int m = start; m < end; ++m) {
        stan::common::print_progress(m, 0, args.get_iter(),
                                     args.get_ctrl_sampling_refresh(), is_warmup,
                                     "\r", "", rstan::io::rcout);
        R_CheckUserInterrupt();
        init_s = sampler_ptr -> transition(init_s);
        if (args.get_ctrl_sampling_save_warmup() && (((m - start) % args.get_ctrl_sampling_thin()) == 0)) {
          outputter.output_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, sampler_ptr, model,
                                        chains, is_warmup,
                                        sampler_params, iter_params,
                                        sum_pars, sum_lp, qoi_idx,
                                        iter_save_i, &rstan::io::rcout);
          iter_save_i++;
          outputter.output_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler_ptr);
        }
      }
    }


Here's Stan's function:
    template <class Model, class RNG>
    void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,
                          int num_iterations,
                          int start,
                          int finish,
                          int num_thin,
                          int refresh,
                          bool save,
                          bool warmup,
                          stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
                          stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
                          Model& model,
                          RNG& base_rng) {
     
      for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {
     
        print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup);
     
        init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);
         
        if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
          writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
          writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
        }

      }
     
    }


I think the sampler->transition() call is the level you're talking about (unless I'm missing something). This is wrapping that call and putting it in a loop and printing where appropriate.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Callbacks in Stan?
parts:
I'd much rather see the callback passed in as a functor
rather than as a C-style function pointer.

So that'd add a template parameter

template <class Model, class RNG, class CB>
...
const CB& c) {
...
c();
}

and then just call the argument as a functor. We'd have
to supply a dummy functor for CmdStan. If you do go with the pointer,
you may just want to check if it's zero and maybe have it
default to 0.

In fact, we should be making the template functionals
for autodiff we're using now constant references instead
of copying them.

Back on topic, here's an example:

#include <iostream>

struct fun {
fun() { }
void operator()() const {
std::cout << "hello" << std::endl;
}
};

template <typename F>
void foo(const F& f) {
f();
}

int main() {
fun callback;
foo(callback);
}

- Bob

On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 3:22 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
I'd much rather see the callback passed in as a functor
rather than as a C-style function pointer.

So that'd add a template parameter

   template <class Model, class RNG, class CB>
   ...
       const CB& c) {
     ...
     c();
   }

and then just call the argument as a functor.  We'd have
to supply a dummy functor for CmdStan.  If you do go with the pointer,
you may just want to check if it's zero and maybe have it
default to 0.

In fact, we should be making the template functionals
for autodiff we're using now constant references instead
of copying them.

Back on topic, here's an example:

#include <iostream>

struct fun {
  fun() { }
  void operator()() const {
    std::cout << "hello" << std::endl;
  }
};

template <typename F>
void foo(const F& f) {
  f();
}

int main() {
  fun callback;
  foo(callback);
}

- Bob

I just realized that if you implement it the way I suggested,
you can also pass in functions!

#include <iostream>

struct fun {
fun() { }
void operator()() const {
std::cout << "hello" << std::endl;
}
};

template <typename F>
void foo(const F& f) {
f();
}

void bar() {
std::cout << "bar" << std::endl;

}

int main() {
fun callback;
foo(callback);

foo(bar);
}


This compiles and prints:

hello
bar

Here's a nice little tutorial:

http://www.cprogramming.com/tutorial/functors-function-objects-in-c++.html

- Bob

> > iter_save_i, &rstan::io::rcout);
> > iter_save_i++;
> > outputter.output_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler_ptr);
> > }
> > }
> > }
> >
> >
> > Here's Stan's function:
> > template <class Model, class RNG>
> > void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,
> > int num_iterations,
> > int start,
> > int finish,
> > int num_thin,
> > int refresh,
> > bool save,
> > bool warmup,
> > stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
> > stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
> > Model& model,
> > RNG& base_rng) {
> >
> > for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {
> >
> > print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup);
> >
> > init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);
> >
> > if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
> > writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
> > writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
> > }
> >
> > }
> >
> > }
> >
> >
> > I think the sampler->transition() call is the level you're talking about (unless I'm missing something). This is wrapping that call and putting it in a loop and printing where appropriate.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 1:31 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > While I don't think a per-iteration null callback function
> > is going to be noticeable speed-wise, I prefer Michael's suggestion
> > to set up the interface so that clients pull iterations rather
> > than inject callbacks.
> >
> > That is, assuming I'm interpreting it right. Rather than
> > generate_warmup_transition(), I'd call it something like
> > get_next_warmup() or get_warmup().
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Mar 12, 2014, at 6:23 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > It should be easy enough to provide API functions for
> > >
> > > initialize
> > > generate_warmup_transition()
> > > generate_sample_transition()
> > >
> > > as well as
> > >
> > > warmup {
> > > for(n in n_samples)
> > > generate_warmup_transition();
> > > }
> > >
> > > and then just have the interfaces ignore the warmup function
> > > if it has to get inside? At least then the code duplication is
> > > minimal.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 5:19 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > > I'll start with the use-case. In RStan, there's a function called 'run_markov_chain()' that mirrors Stan's function. I'd post the code, but it's not really useful as is. The substantive difference between the two functions is that RStan has one additional line:
> > >
> > > R_CheckUserInterrupt();
> > >
> > > RStan calls that function to check whether or not the user has interrupted the process within a for loop. (For the time being, I'm going to ignore the danger in leaving dangling resources. This is how RStan currently works now and I'm just trying to refactor the code so we share more common code.)
> > >
> > > My question is, should I just add a function pointer to the method to deal with this interrupt handler? Is there a different pattern we should adopt to make it cleaner?
> > >
> > > Is this going to introduce too much overhead? What's the cleanest way to deal with an empty function? CmdStan doesn't need this call, so what should we do about it? Do I create two functions in Stan to maintain efficiency at the cost of duplicating code (one with and without this argument)?
> > >
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
